---
title: "Learn analog design through current balance"
---

An analog circuit is a set of connected devices that must agree on currents
and voltages. This route starts with one transistor, builds a useful amplifier,
then follows mirrors, differential operation, feedback, uncertainty and supply
interfaces toward the questions an LDO would need answered. Each chapter connects
an estimate, selected observations and a design judgment.

**Learning edition v1.5.** The English chapters are the canonical route; the
[Japanese reading overview](../ja/learning-path.qmd) explains where to begin
and how the evidence fits. The five detailed studies remain available with
their original circuit files, definitions, downloads and results.

The route develops the worked current/gm/width argument and measured
mirror/headroom limits. Its separately planned **initial-D1 5/25-pF example**
shows why a larger receiving capacitor slows response without repairing DC
tracking error. This increment uses that result to forecast and check a
12-versus-15-pF choice against an illustrative deadline. It also derives the
finite reference's supply-error path and explains a narrower distribution
with fewer fixed-window passes. The finite-signal explanation now connects
independent saved DC curvature to harmonics, actual gate/source motion and
input-current costs. Chapter 6 then traces one resistor’s noise through both
of its terminals and quantifies the passive noise cost. A two-condition
common-mode example then tests why an output clamp's current capability does
not define the input range of a buffer. It connects changed tail headroom,
unequal input paths and weaker feedback response. All previous exact downloads
remain available.

## The reading order

| Read | What you will be able to decide |
| --- | --- |
| [1. MOS operating point and sizing](01-mos-operating-point.qmd) | What current, headroom, dimensions and local derivatives tell you about a device. |
| [2. Common-source amplifier](02-common-source.qmd) | How MOS behavior and a resistor load jointly set the center, gain and finite swing. |
| [3. Mirrors and bias](03-mirrors-and-bias.qmd) | How a finite reference establishes load current, and why signal gain does not measure DC accuracy. |
| [4. Differential pair and OTA](04-differential-pair-and-ota.qmd) | How two inputs steer current; what changes when a clamped OTA becomes a buffer. |
| [5. Feedback and response](05-feedback-and-response.qmd) | Part A: connection, loading and precision. Part B: bandwidth, settling, slew and recovery. |
| [6. Errors and resources](06-errors-and-resources.qmd) | How to separate noise, offset, variation and error transmission before spending current or area. |
| [7. Supply and startup](07-supply-and-startup.qmd) | What the supply, reference and input must deliver or absorb through declared histories. |
| [8. Toward an LDO](08-toward-an-ldo.qmd) | Which interfaces these blocks support, and what a regulator still needs demonstrated. |

Read 1–4 in order if these circuits are new. Chapter 5 has two reading stops;
understand its connections before its dynamic measurements. Experienced readers
can use the table to enter at a design question, then follow each chapter's
links to the exact supporting study. No simulator installation is needed to
read the route or inspect its plots and compact source data.

## A small notation toolkit

**Kirchhoff's current law (KCL):** signed currents entering a node sum to zero.
At an output with a load capacitor, current imbalance changes stored charge:
$I_{in}-I_{out}=C\,dV/dt$. At stationary DC, that capacitor current is zero.
**Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL):** voltage changes around a closed path sum to
zero. We usually implement it by naming node voltages relative to `0`, the
chosen ground reference, and subtracting them: $V_{GS}=V_G-V_S$.

A MOS reading view always names **D**rain, **G**ate, **S**ource and **B**ody:

```text
N0(D=out, G=gate, S=source, B=0) W=... L=...
Rload(out, 0) = ...
```

The node names show connectivity; device names distinguish physical instances.
`N0` denotes an NMOS and `P0` a PMOS in these reading views. The exact linked
SPICE, including zero-volt current sensors, is the execution authority. Text
views explain a circuit and need not compile as SV/AMS. A body connection is
part of the circuit, not a cosmetic choice. Width and length are in µm in the
reading tables, and metres where the model's input schema requires them.

Upper-case $V_O$ denotes a DC output operating point; lower-case $v_o$ denotes
a small change about it. An AC analysis solves a linearized circuit at that
point. A time-domain analysis follows a finite waveform; it can show distortion,
charging limits and a changed operating region that the linearization misses.
Never add a nominal DC voltage to an AC gain as though they were the same kind
of quantity.

## Predict, inspect, then judge

A calculation is most useful when its assumptions can fail visibly. For example,
gain might initially be estimated from transconductance times output resistance.
The next question is which load, source motion or bias branch that estimate
omitted. A more elaborate circuit earns its cost only if it improves the
required function under the relevant conditions.

Here **observed** means a saved simulator observation with a stated model,
circuit and stimulus. A **first estimate** uses a stated approximation without
the target result. A **retrospective explanation** uses an already observed
operating point or response—for example, inserting saved gm and gds into a
node equation to explain the saved amplifier gain. A **prospective prediction**
records its inputs and forecast before observing its declared target. These
roles are different even when they use the same equation.

**Confirmation** refers to the original studies' frozen finite experiments;
their samples are already known evidence for this learning edition. Rewriting
an explanation does not make its old targets unexposed again. A nominal example
is not a population result, and a valid computation can represent a circuit
that fails its performance requirement.

Noise needs a bandwidth and a reference port. DC variation needs a physical
realization model. The two are introduced where first used and brought together
in chapter 6. The model is pinned APM v5.0.0/APM045 VTG with ngspice 47; these
results do not establish foundry statistics, manufacturing yield, layout/PEX
performance or silicon qualification. The [methods page](../methods.qmd) explains
the evidence and review limits.

## Keep the depth and the reproduction routes

The [five studies](../index.qmd#detailed-studies) retain complete design guides,
failure records, original measurement definitions and exact downloads. The
[learning evidence package](../studies/learning-path-v1/reproduce.qmd) adds the
four selected archived differential-pair/OTA cases, current-balance calculations
and figure regeneration. It supplies the selected public inputs; reading or
replaying them does not require access to the private research archive.

The [learning-day supplement](../studies/learning-day-v1/reproduce.qmd) adds
selected historical sizing/mirror observations and the nine declared nominal
receiving-port cases, with separate graph calculations and a public 25-pF
OP/AC/step replay. Its new identifiers preserve the first package's bytes and
the distinction between archival explanation and newly planned observation.

The [design-decisions supplement](../studies/learning-decisions-v1/reproduce.qmd)
adds the supply/loss recalculation from the original public feedback ZIP and
the two predeclared capacitor choices. It supplies three further graphs and
one native 12-pF replay. The worked local supply estimate uses known OP data;
the 12/15-pF forecasts were recorded before their later target conditions.

The [signal explanation](../studies/learning-signal-v1/reproduce.qmd) adds
six known sine cycles, eight selected static observations, two graphs and
a known-input native F75L example. Its local curvature check is independent
of the waveform-derived estimate; both are retrospective uses of old data.
The original eight-cycle THD and the new single-cycle decomposition remain
separate measurements.

The [resistor-noise supplement](../studies/learning-noise-v1/reproduce.qmd)
adds the selected complex output-current transfers, partial noise calculation
and graph. One predeclared direct branch-current diagnostic checks the
coherent two-terminal path; its public replay needs one OP and one AC sweep.
The existing total-noise observations remain separate from that new path test.

The [common-mode supplement](../studies/learning-common-mode-v1/reproduce.qmd)
adds two initial-core OP/AC conditions, a separate retrospective node calculation,
one figure and a known-input high-command D1 replay. It retains the failed
large-range local extrapolation and distinguishes a buffer's moving input from
an LDO's separately specified sense/reference and control ports.

The progression is informed by the device–diode–amplifier–mirror–pair–OTA order
in [Pretl, Koefinger and Dorrer's course](https://iic-jku.github.io/analog-circuit-design/aicd.html)
and by [Wulff's circuit](https://analogicus.com/aic2026/circuits),
[OTA](https://analogicus.com/aic2026/otas) and
[regulator](https://analogicus.com/aic2026/voltage_regulation) discussions.
Those are valuable further reading in their own process and teaching context.
The prose, circuit observations and comparisons in this route are original;
upstream dimensions or statistical assumptions are not transferred to APM.

Begin with [what the MOS operating point tells you](01-mos-operating-point.qmd).
